title: Integer Promotion & Type Conversions
html:
Before most arithmetic, C silently converts operands: small integers are promoted to int, and mixed types are brought to a common type. Signed/unsigned mixing is the classic source of bugs.

Integer promotion

Any char, short or bit-field (signed or unsigned) used in an expression is first converted to int (or unsigned int if int can’t hold all its values).

The usual arithmetic conversions

1
Any floating operand?
Convert the other to the widest floating type involved (long double > double > float).
2
Otherwise promote
Apply integer promotion to both operands.
3
Same signedness
Convert to the higher-rank type (int < long < long long).
4
Mixed signedness
If the unsigned type has rank ≥ the signed one, the signed operand becomes unsigned. Otherwise, if the signed type can represent every unsigned value, convert to the signed type; else to its unsigned counterpart.

Clang warns about the implicit version of this comparison (-Wsign-compare, part of -Wextra) — one more reason to keep warnings on:

Explicit casts and narrowing

ConversionResult
Any integer → unsigned typeWell defined: value modulo 2ᴺ
Out-of-range integer → signed typeImplementation-defined (wraps on all real compilers; C23 mandates two’s complement)
Floating → integerTruncates toward zero; UB if the value doesn’t fit
Integer → floatingMay lose precision for large values
double → floatRounded; UB/inf if out of range
Why does (unsigned char)255 + 1 give 256 and not 0?

Because of integer promotion: the unsigned char operand is promoted to int before the addition, so the arithmetic is done in int. The result only wraps to 0 if it is stored back into an unsigned char.

What is the result of -1 < 0u?

0 (false). -1 is converted to unsigned int (becoming UINT_MAX) because both operands have the same rank and one is unsigned. This is why comparing an int with strlen() or sizeof can go wrong.
